title: Do AI agents for crypto trading actually work, or is it mostly hype?
author: alittlebitnostalgic
selftext:
I use AI for basic normal stuffs with respect to trading like getting a market overviews, checking if my trade thesis makes sense or sometimes just catching up on news.  
  
Recently I've been seeing a lot of people talk about AI agents that can actually place trades onchain and manage positions for you, end to end. Some people swear by them while some say it's just another way to lose money lol.  
  
I'm kinda eager to try them out but also a lil sceptical about letting an agent trade with my money. Like using AI for research is fine, but trusting it with actual trades? Idk about that yet.  
  
Anyone here who's tried these AI trading agents ? How's the experience been, and where would you even start without risking much?

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
They work in the narrow sense that they place the trades. Whether the trades are any good is a separate question, and most of what you're seeing is people posting a good week.

Where I'd start: run one on a testnet or with fake money for a month and read every trade it made and the reason it gave. You'll learn more from the dumb ones than the good ones.

If you go live after that, give it a key that can trade but can't withdraw, on an account holding only what you'd shrug off losing, and set a hard daily loss limit at the exchange, outside the agent. Don't let the agent be the thing that decides when the agent stops.

The research use you already have is where most of the value sits anyway.

comments.author: Abject_Disaster7292
comments.body:
Where it’s genuinely useful is spotting opportunities a newer trader would miss. Mine scans the whole watchlist several times a day, checks the news on anything that’s moving, and writes down why it took or skipped each one. Even on days it doesn’t trade, reading why it passed on something taught me a lot.



The other surprise is how often it says no. Most scans end with no trade, because it sticks to the rules even when I’d want to jump in. That discipline is honestly the main value.



If you try one, start with a small amount you’re fine losing, write clear rules for it, and read its logs every day for the first few weeks. Mine had a bug once that I only caught because I was reading the logs.

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body:
Where I've seen it make sense is splitting the jobs. Let the model do the reading and summarizing, and keep entries, sizing and stops as plain rules in code it can't touch. Most blowups I read about come from the model deciding its own size or moving its own stop.

To start cheap, run it on paper with the exact same order path you'd use live, and log the reason for every trade. After a few weeks compare it to a dumb baseline like buy and hold or a simple SMA cross over the same period.

If it can't beat that after fees, you found out for free.

comments.author: Visible_Let_7292
comments.body:
I think the sensible way to start is to give an agent a small separate wallet and see how it handles actual trades before automating anything.

For context, I am affiliated with Wayfinder. Their Shells (agents) can operate with dedicated wallets, and the hosted agent doesn't directly hold your private keys. You can fund a wallet with just what you're comfortable testing and keep your main funds separate.

That should help with your concern about trusting an agent with real money, since you're only risking what you've set aside to test it.

You can also use it to research trades, check market data, place trades with your approval & track your open positions and PnL, all in one place.

I'd personally start with a few small trades and see how the agent handles intricacies like execution, fees and position management before giving it more control.

imo, that's prolly a better way to judge how useful it actually is.

comments.author: 0utlawViking
comments.body: I'm curious about this too, using ai for research is one thing but trusting it with actual trades feels like a different game I'd probably start with paper trading and see how it perform before putting money in it.
